Pharmacodynamics The drug label provides limited information regarding the pharmacodynamics of esterified estrogens. Pharmacokinetics Distribution: The distribution of exogenous estrogens is similar to that of endogenous estrogens. Estrogens are widely distributed throughout the body and are typically found in higher concentrations in target organs of sex hormones. In the bloodstream, estrogens primarily circulate bound to sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and albumin. Metabolism: Exogenous estrogens are metabolized in the same manner as endogenous estrogens. Circulating estrogens exist in a dynamic equilibrium of metabolic interconversions. These transformations predominantly occur in the liver. Estradiol is reversibly converted to estrone, and both can be further converted to estriol, which is the primary urinary metabolite. Estrogens also undergo enterohepatic recirculation through sulfate and glucuronide conjugation in the liver, biliary secretion of these conjugates into the intestine, and subsequent hydrolysis in the gut followed by reabsorption. In postmenopausal women, a significant proportion of circulating estrogens exist as sulfate conjugates, particularly estrone sulfate, which serves as a circulating reservoir for the formation of more active estrogens. Excretion: Estradiol, estrone, and estriol are excreted in the urine, along with their glucuronide and sulfate conjugates. Drug Interactions: Both in vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that estrogens are partially metabolized by the cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) enzyme. Consequently, inducers or inhibitors of CYP3A4 can influence the metabolism of estrogen drugs. CYP3A4 inducers, such as St. John’s Wort (Hypericum perforatum), phenobarbital, carbamazepine, and rifampin, may reduce plasma concentrations of estrogens, potentially leading to decreased therapeutic effects and/or alterations in uterine bleeding patterns. CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, and grapefruit juice, may increase plasma concentrations of estrogens, potentially resulting in an increased risk of side effects. Nonclinical Toxicology Long-term continuous administration of estrogen, with or without progestin, in women with or without a uterus, has been associated with an increased risk of endometrial cancer, breast cancer, and ovarian cancer. In certain animal species, prolonged administration of natural and synthetic estrogens has been shown to increase the frequency of carcinomas in the breast, uterus, cervix, vagina, testis, and liver. A study evaluating the effects of 5 mg medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) per day compared to placebo for the prevention of certain chronic diseases identified coronary heart disease (CHD) as the primary endpoint. CHD was defined as nonfatal myocardial infarction and CHD-related death, with invasive breast cancer as the primary adverse outcome studied. A “global index” was used to include the earliest occurrence of CHD, invasive breast cancer, stroke, pulmonary embolism (PE), endometrial cancer, colorectal cancer, hip fracture, or death due to other causes. The study did not assess the effects of conjugated estrogens (CE) or CE/MPA on menopausal symptoms. The absolute excess risks per 10,000 women-years in the CE/MPA-treated group included: 7 more CHD events, 8 more strokes, 8 more PEs, and 8 more invasive breast cancers. The absolute risk reductions per 10,000 women-years included: 6 fewer colorectal cancers and 5 fewer hip fractures. The overall absolute excess risk of events included in the “global index” was 19 per 10,000 women-years.
